headline_marked: [[19th-century Stirling Engine cools AMD Threadripper]] chipset, converting waste heat into mechanical work
headline: 19th-century Stirling Engine cools AMD Threadripper chipset, converting waste heat into mechanical work
summary: Windows guru Dave W. Plummer demonstrated using a $40 Stirling Engine to passively cool his Threadripper 3970X, spinning a flywheel from the chipset's waste heat.
details: Windows developer Dave W. Plummer showcased a unique cooling method for his AMD Threadripper chipset. He used a low-temperature Stirling Engine, typically found in educational models, to convert the chipset's waste heat into mechanical energy, spinning a flywheel.

The Stirling Engine, patented in 1816, operates by converting heat energy into mechanical work through a closed-cycle process. A heat source expands gas, which drives a piston and turns a flywheel, then cools the gas.

The specific engine used appears to be a Sunnytech Low Temperature Stirling Engine, available for around $40. These engines are sensitive enough to spin from the heat of a hot beverage or even a hand, making a Threadripper chipset a viable heat source.

While not a primary cooling solution, the demonstration highlights an interesting application of classic physics. Plummer's video shows the engine in action, though specific temperature data or benchmark improvements are yet to be shared.

Further details, including potential performance impacts, are anticipated in a longer video on Dave's Garage YouTube channel. This experiment offers a novel, albeit unconventional, approach to managing component heat.

headline_marked: [[CodeZero's new canary release]] brings AI flow generation, new module system
headline: CodeZero's new canary release brings AI flow generation, new module system
summary: CodeZero's latest canary release introduces AI-powered flow generation, a new module system, and an improved execution results view in the IDE, marking a significant step for backend automation.
details: CodeZero's latest canary release introduces AI-powered flow generation, a new module system, and an enhanced execution results view in the IDE. This update marks a significant step, bringing artificial intelligence to the platform for the first time.

Users can now describe desired automations, select an AI model, and watch flows build in real-time. This aims to make backend automation accessible to everyone, regardless of their preference for visual building or plain language descriptions.

The entire platform has been restructured around modules, bundling functions, flow types, and data types for clearer project capabilities. This provides a tidier, more intuitive building experience that scales with projects.

A new execution results view in the IDE shows step-by-step outcomes of every run, simplifying problem diagnosis and fixing. Results are saved for revisiting, and the groundwork for test executions has been laid.

The IDE also received new input fields for text, numbers, toggles, and selections, alongside a reworked suggestion menu with tabs and search. A new license management page simplifies Enterprise Edition license handling for self-managed installations.

Reliability improvements include runtimes continuously reporting health for immediate detection of unresponsive services. External service connections are more secure with new authentication options, and numerous fixes enhance stability.
